The updated clinical impression introduces two critical red flags for malignancy: **progressive painless jaundice** and **unintentional weight loss of 6.3 kg**, which meets formal oncologic criteria (≥5% body weight loss over 6–12 months). These symptoms — especially in combination with obstructive jaundice — dramatically shift the pretest probability away from benign cystic lesions (e.g., simple choledochal cyst) and toward **malignant biliary obstruction**. While choledochal cysts can rarely undergo malignant transformation, they almost never present *de novo* in adulthood with weight loss and progressive painless jaundice; they typically manifest earlier in life (often childhood/young adulthood) with intermittent abdominal pain, cholangitis, or pancreatitis — none of which are reported here. In contrast, **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) of the pancreatic head** is the *most common cause of painless jaundice with weight loss and bile duct dilation* in adults. Critically, the summary now specifies *proximal* extrahepatic obstruction (i.e., obstruction at or near the hilum or upper CBD), yet also describes a *subhepatic* cystic mass — an apparent anatomical contradiction unless the mass is large enough to extend upward or the obstruction is multifocal. However, the phrase “proximal extrahepatic biliary obstruction” may reflect mischaracterization: intrahepatic duct dilation *plus* a subhepatic mass is far more consistent with *distal* obstruction (as upstream pressure propagates retrograde). The most parsimonious explanation reconciling *all* data — painless jaundice, weight loss, intrahepatic duct dilation, subhepatic cystic lesion, and high suspicion for malignancy — is **a cystic or partially cystic malignancy in the periampullary region**, with **pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)** remaining the most prevalent diagnosis in this demographic and presentation.
